defaults.permitted_development: Across Tyne and Wear, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, height control for a roof-light is simple but strict: the proposal should not rise above the existing roof. The more flush and subordinate the unit appears, the easier the scheme is to keep within the normal householder route.
rules.depth_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, a roof-light is easiest to defend when it remains subordinate to the slope and does not slide into dormer or terrace territory. Once the wider roof form changes materially, the normal roof-light route no longer tells the full story.
rules.materials_rules: Across Tyne and Wear, choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Roof-lights in listed buildings are commonly treated as heritage works because the roof covering, structure and external appearance all contribute to significance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Roof-specific planning conditions and Article 4 directions are a common reason why an otherwise modest roof-light still needs planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: For houses in Newcastle upon Tyne, the usual roof-light route is to keep the unit modest: no more than 150mm projection from the existing roof slope and no increase above the existing roof height. Once the proposal sits on a more sensitive roofscape or forms part of a larger roof alteration, planning permission is more likely to be needed.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.
rules.depth_rules: The unit must not project more than 150 millimetres from the plane of the existing roof slope. Once the projection starts to read as a box, dormer or raised roof feature, the simpler roof-light route usually stops applying.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: Roof-lights are treated as minor roof alterations, not full roof enlargements, so the existing roof form should remain dominant. Roof terraces, raised platforms and larger roof additions sit outside the normal roof-light route.
rules.materials_rules: Use flashings, frame colours and glazing details that sit quietly within the existing roof. The closer the finish is to the host roof covering and the less bulky the frame, the easier it is to keep the alteration visually subordinate.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status makes roof-lights more sensitive on visible elevations, particularly where a simple modern unit would cut across a traditional roof pattern.
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building roof usually needs a heritage-led approach: even a small roof-light can require consent if it affects the historic fabric or appearance.
restrictions.article4_notes: A local Article 4 direction or earlier planning condition can take away the normal roof-light permitted development route, particularly on prominent roof slopes.

rules.permitted_development: In North Tyneside, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.

rules.depth_rules: Projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.

rules.roof_rules: The proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Materials are not just about weathering: they control how visible the roof-light looks. Neat flashings, restrained frame colours and a low-profile unit usually sit better than bright trims or bulky cassettes.

rules.height_rules: The roof-light should not make any part of the roof higher than it is now. A low-profile installation that leaves the original roof form dominant is generally the strongest option.
rules.depth_rules: Projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: If the proposal creates a side-facing window, it should be obscure-glazed and any opening part should have its lowest edge at least 1.7 metres above the floor level of the room. Privacy and visible road-facing roof slopes deserve the earliest check.
rules.roof_rules: A roof-light is easiest to defend when it remains subordinate to the slope and does not slide into dormer or terrace territory. Once the wider roof form changes materially, the normal roof-light route no longer tells the full story.
rules.materials_rules: The best material strategy is usually visual restraint. Low-profile frames and clean flashings that work with the existing roof covering are less likely to jar with the roofscape than chunky or highly contrasting units.
